item.title: The Daily Star – Bangladesh is building factories. Who will run their supply chains?
item.description:
Walk into the operations office of almost any large manufacturer in Bangladesh, including multinationals, and you will find a familiar pattern. The workers on the factory floor are Bangladeshi. The technicians keeping critical machines running are often from Sri Lanka. The managers planning production, sourcing inputs and moving goods are frequently from India, and so, typically, are the general managers. I have seen this first-hand at a US multinational operating here. After decades as one of the world's manufacturing nations, we still import the people who run our supply chains.

That gap is about to become far more expensive.

A bigger, harder industrial bet

Ready-made garments account for 80–83 per cent of our exports and employ some 4.4 million people. The country is now making a deliberate, capital-backed push into pharmaceuticals and active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), electronics, light engineering and technical textiles.
A worker operates pharmaceutical processing equipment at a facility in Tongi. As Bangladesh expands into pharmaceuticals and active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), the industry will need skilled professionals to manage complex supply chains, source regulated inputs from multiple countries and maintain international quality standards. Photo: Rashed Shumon

The numbers are not small. The National Special Economic Zone at Mirsharai–Sitakunda–Sonagazi, the Japanese Economic Zone under development in Araihazar, the Chinese Economic Zone in Anwara and several existing and new EPZs together report hundreds of factories and multibillion-dollar proposed investments. Foreign direct investment rose by 45 per cent in 2025 as global firms looked for 'China+1' alternatives. Government policy targets a 40 per cent increase in light engineering's contribution to GDP by 2027 and aims to replace a $1.3 billion annual API import bill with local production.

Every one of these sectors is far more supply-chain-intensive than the cut-and-sew process. A pharmaceutical plant must source regulated inputs from several countries, maintain traceability and pass foreign audits. An electronics assembler juggles thousands of components across multi-tier supplier networks. Getting a container through Chattogram port, customs and multiple agency approvals on time is a management discipline in itself. These industries need people who understand the supply chain end to end: complex demand and supply planning, inventory management, running complex warehouses, working out and optimising air, sea, rail and road logistics, negotiating with global suppliers, and using data analytics and AI to do all of it better. Without them, the factories in our economic zones will surely underperform, or investors will fly in their own managers, as many do today.

The clock, deferred or not

Bangladesh was scheduled to graduate from Least Developed Country (LDC) status on 24 November 2026. However, the UN General Assembly, at its most recent session, extended the preparatory period to November 2029.

When graduation occurs, duty-free access to the EU and other markets will be phased out, and tariffs on key products will rise. The only durable answer is to become efficient enough to compete without preferences. Our labour productivity is about $8.7 per hour, compared with $12.4 in Vietnam and $19.8 in China. Closing that gap is partly about machines. It is largely about skilled management.

An extension is not a reprieve. It is three years, exactly the time it takes to build a serious graduate programme and graduate its first class.
Students and instructors examine textile machinery at the BUBT textile laboratory. As Bangladesh expands into technical textiles and other industries, it needs professionals who understand complex supply chains, from production planning and inventory management to logistics. File Photo.

What our universities offer today

Bangladesh's private universities have grown impressively, but their supply chain offerings are limited. AIUB has an Operations and Supply Chain Management department offering BBA and MBA concentrations. BRAC University has a Master's in Procurement & Supply Management (MPSM) programme. A few others offer MBA majors with courses on supply chain management.

There is not a single dedicated, industry-facing master's degree (MS) in supply chain management in the country. Meanwhile, our best BBA and MBA graduates gravitate towards banks, telecoms and marketing, or jobs abroad. A factory or manufacturing company is rarely seen as a career destination for the brightest. That has created a huge talent gap.

Others have noticed. Malaysia's UCSI University already markets its supply chain master's programme directly to Bangladeshi students. When a foreign university is selling into your market, the demand is real, and the first-mover advantage for local universities will quickly disappear.

What our competitors did

Malaysia partnered with MIT's Center for Transportation and Logistics to create the Malaysia Institute for Supply Chain Innovation, whose 10-month master's programme was ranked first in the world by Eduniversal in 2021. India runs dedicated supply chain MBAs at IIM Udaipur and IIM Mumbai, backed by its National Logistics Policy.

Vietnam offers a warning. It has many bachelor's programmes, yet its own industry reports that only 5–7 per cent of its logistics workforce has formal training.

The leading US programmes at MIT, Michigan State, Arizona State, the University of Tennessee and USC share a common approach: a real capstone project with a sponsoring company, end-to-end coverage from procurement to analytics, small cohorts, and AI woven into core courses. Writing the syllabus is the easy part. Building the industry partnerships that turn capstones into hiring pipelines is the hard part, and here Bangladesh has an unusual advantage. Hundreds of investors are setting up inside our economic zones right now. A programme built around capstone partnerships with those companies would be distinctive from day one.

Three asks of university leadership

First, decide. Several private universities are well placed. Some have the brand and accreditation record to meet international standards; some already offer supply-chain-related degrees or courses. What is missing is not capacity but a vice-chancellor or dean willing to take ownership of the programme and build a centre of excellence in operations and supply chain management.

Second, borrow credibility. Partner with an established international programme rather than start from zero. And tap into the diaspora: senior Bangladeshi-origin supply chain academics teach in Australia and the UK, and at least one has already come home to lead a university here.
Workers operate machinery inside a factory at the Korean Export Processing Zone in Anwara and West Patiya, Chattogram. Ready-made garments account for 80–83 percent of Bangladesh's exports and employ some 4.4 million people, but the country's emerging industries will require far more complex supply chain management. Photo: Star

Third, start the clock. Getting from a firm decision to the first graduating cohort takes roughly 32–36 months: about three months to commit, six months to design the curriculum and submit it to the UGC, four months to secure approval, hire faculty and sign up capstone sponsors, followed by an 18-month programme.

Government policymakers and industry have roles too. BIDA has streamlined the investment process through Invest Bangladesh. Invest Bangladesh should now treat professional talent as investment infrastructure, as Thailand did with its Eastern Economic Corridor, by offering co-funded scholarships and tax incentives for companies that sponsor students. Manufacturers who complain about the skills gap should sponsor capstone projects and hire graduates of these programmes. Nor is this a job for private universities alone: BUET and the larger public universities should also take the coming talent gap seriously and begin developing their own plans.

Why now

The new deadline for LDC graduation is November 2029. A university that commits this year can graduate its first cohort in early 2030, just as preferences begin to lapse and the economic zones reach scale. If we can supply only blue-collar labour to these economic zones, and not the professionals who run them, the whole diversification effort will stall before it starts.

We have proven we can make clothes for the world. The question now is whether we can manage the far more complex supply chains our new industries demand, or whether we will keep importing the talent.

Reza Kibria is an independent adviser to NGOs, higher education institutions and start-ups. He has three decades of supply chain management experience with US multinational companies and, most recently, spent five years with the USC Marshall School of Business in Los Angeles. He can be reached at [email protected].

item.title: The Daily Star – Maulana Bhashani in Assam, 1928–1947 : Peasants in the national liberation movement
item.description:
‘The peasantry is systematically disregarded for the most part by the propaganda put out by the nationalist parties.’ (Fanon, 1990: 47)

Frantz Fanon (1925–1961) participated in Algeria’s struggle for independence. Long before the Liberation War of 1971, the peasants of Bangladesh had experienced much the same thing. A consideration of Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani’s life also compels us to acknowledge the truth of Fanon’s observation. In this brief essay, I shall confine myself to highlighting this particular lesson.

The life of Maulana Bhashani is, in a sense, the story of Bangladesh’s Muslim peasantry, commonly known as Bengali Muslims.

By a stroke of fortune, he remained largely beyond the reach of colonial education. It seems that the corrupting influence of that education could not entirely diminish his extraordinary character. On numerous occasions, he unmasked the principal comprador or collaborating classes, including landlords, the newly wealthy and the middle classes. He began this work long before the Partition of India, in the province of Assam in undivided India. His name remains unforgettable among the leading figures of the struggle for independence achieved in 1947.

Yet Maulana Bhashani’s contribution to the struggle for independence in 1947 was, in one way or another, erased from the histories written in subsequent decades. This was true not only in the new India but also in the newly established Pakistan. Indeed, apart from a handful of scattered essays, his achievements have remained largely unknown to the wider public to this day.

In this essay, I shall offer only a brief account of Maulana Bhashani’s life, particularly his political career, which began in the province of Assam in undivided India. A comprehensive examination of all its dimensions lies beyond the scope of my knowledge.

I

In 1971, faced with attacks by the Pakistani military, Maulana Bhashani sought refuge in India. Among those who accompanied him was Saiful Islam, a left-wing political activist from the Pabna–Sirajganj region. Indeed, during their wartime exile, he also served as the Maulana’s personal assistant. In 1987, he published some of his recollections and experiences in a volume entitled Swadhinata Bhashani Bharat (Independence, Bhashani and India). About a decade and a half later, around 2002, he published another booklet with the rather cumbersome title Assam O Maulana Bhashani Ebong Line Protha-Bangalkheda (Assam, Maulana Bhashani, the Line System and the Expulsion of Bengalis). This booklet, too, drew upon his experiences of 1971. In it, he attributed many statements directly to Maulana Bhashani, although he did not always specify where or when the Maulana had made them.

As I began reading the booklet, I found myself confronted with a question: Why, and for what reasons, had Maulana Bhashani joined the Pakistan Movement? The answer is not straightforward. Nor does Saiful Islam offer any particularly illuminating answer to this question. I recalled that he, too, belonged to those generally described as leftists in our country. Regrettably, I found that only by carefully considering his various observations might one arrive at something resembling an answer.
Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani attends a meeting of the advisory committee of the Bangladesh government-in-exile during the Liberation War of 1971, alongside Tajuddin Ahmad, Professor Muzaffar Ahmad, Monoranjan Dhar, Comrade Moni Singh and other leaders.

Saiful Islam frequently made a point of telling others that, although he enjoyed a good personal relationship with Maulana Bhashani, he did not consider the Maulana’s politics to be correct. At one point in his booklet, Maulana Bhashani O Assam Ebong Line Protha-Bangalkheda, Saiful Islam writes explicitly:

‘I could not agree with him about the involvement of religion in discussion, reasoning, movements, rebellions and revolutions. It was for this reason that, despite having a good personal relationship with Maulana Bhashani, I could not remain politically associated with him’ (Islam, 2003: 25).

Now, in 1971, while Bangladesh’s Liberation War was under way, Saiful Islam asked Maulana Bhashani, as they sat on the soil of Bhashan Char in Assam: ‘Why did you transform the non-communal movement against the Line System in Assam into the communal Pakistan Movement?’ In response, Maulana Bhashani invoked the egalitarian and other positive dimensions of religion.

Saiful Islam had his own convictions. Why would he listen to arguments about religion? The problem lay within his own assumptions. Even before posing the question, he already knew what he expected the answer to be. He had taken it for granted that ‘Pakistan’ was a ‘communal’ phenomenon, or merely another name for communalism. He had no real interest in discovering whether there was anything more to it.

It is true that he did not receive the answer he had hoped for. Yet another kind of answer presented itself to him through an actual event. He failed, however, to recognise that the event itself contained an answer to his question. The Pakistan Movement was not merely a communal movement; it was also a form of national movement.

An examination of the experience of the broad-based popular movement organised under Maulana Bhashani’s leadership to abolish the Line System, introduced by the British colonial government to restrict the settlement of Bengali Muslim peasants in Assam, would likewise demonstrate that the parties leading, or claiming to lead, struggles for national independence have consistently been reluctant to recognise peasant movements as either the foundation of, or participants in, national movements.

Saiful Islam recounts that, at one point during their stay in a refugee camp in India in 1971, Maulana Bhashani expressed a personal wish. He wanted to meet his disciples one last time. There was only one way to bring thousands of his disciples together: to organise an urs, a religious gathering.

According to Saiful Islam’s account, arrangements were made to hold the urs at Bhashan Char. Throughout the night, the disciples engaged in zikr and other devotional recitations. The following day, a vast public gathering took place, with Maulana Bhashani as its sole speaker. Addressing the assembled disciples, followers and members of the wider public, he described the appalling acts of irreligion committed by the Pakistanis in the name of religion. At the same time, he made a point of emphasising the secular character of Bangladesh’s national struggle, that is, its universal appeal.

I have summarised Saiful Islam’s testimony above in my own customary language. I shall now reproduce his observations in his own words:

‘I came to understand that Muslims in India were not supportive of Bangladesh’s struggle for independence, both from my travels through Calcutta, Cooch Behar, Delhi, Dehradun, Ajmer and other places, and from my experiences in Assam. But during Maulana Bhashani’s speech, as I moved around the public gathering, listening to conversations among his disciples of different ages, I repeatedly heard one sentiment expressed: “Huzur wanted Pakistan, so we voted for Pakistan. Now that he no longer wants Pakistan, there must be some deeper wisdom in this.” After the public meeting, I saw that the people departed with an anti-Pakistan outlook’ (Islam, 2003: 25).
This undated photo shows Maulana Bhashani holding a portrait of Lenin. Source:sputnikimages.com

II

Everyone knows that Maulana Bhashani’s original name was Abdul Hamid Khan. Where did this name come from? Those familiar with what is known as the ‘Bengali Muslim mind’ will know that he was named after the Ottoman Sultan Abdul Hamid II, whom Bengali Muslims regarded as the Caliph of Islam. We cannot say with certainty whether Maulana Bhashani was born in 1880 or 1885. We can, however, say that our Abdul Hamid’s life began during the reign of the Ottoman Sultan-Caliph Abdul Hamid II (1876–1909). As for the name by which he became famous throughout the world, ‘Bhashani’, he acquired it from Bhashan Char in Goalpara district of Assam. He was indebted to Assam not merely for the name ‘Bhashani’, but also for his life, youth, wealth and honour. And the people of Bangladesh, in turn, owe him a debt for the independence achieved in 1947.

Who, in principle, can be regarded as the true leader of Bengali Muslims? Before any other name comes to mind, there is that of Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani.

This is no small matter. Around the time of his birth, poor peasants from northern Bengal had begun migrating to Assam, particularly the Brahmaputra Valley, where they cultivated previously uncultivated land and established new settlements. This migration was directly connected to British colonial rule. Of those who embarked upon this arduous and hazardous undertaking with the encouragement of the British ruling authorities, the overwhelming majority, an estimated 85 per cent, were Muslims from eastern Bengal.

In 1905, Assam was joined with Eastern Bengal to form a new province. It should be remembered that 30 years earlier, in 1874, Sylhet district had been separated from Bengal and incorporated into Assam. I have heard many emotionally inclined writers describe this event as the ‘first partition of Bengal’. Even after the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam was abolished in 1911, the Muslim-majority district of Sylhet remained part of Assam. As everyone knows, the whole of Sylhet district remained within Assam until 1947. Karimganj subdivision remains in Assam to this day.

Assam’s long-established Assamese Muslim community constituted a minority. Even before the twentieth century, the Muslim population of Assam had begun to grow across both the Brahmaputra Valley in the west and the Surma Valley in the east. This development provoked two kinds of reaction: one from Assam’s established population and the other from the British rulers, particularly the owners of tea plantations. The growing Bengali Muslim population in Assam came to be perceived as a new threat.

Around 1916, discussions began about whether restrictions could be imposed to prevent peasants from eastern Bengal from settling throughout Assam. In 1920, a regulation was introduced under which designated lines or boundaries were drawn in certain districts. Peasants arriving from Bengal were prohibited from settling beyond these lines. This was the famous Line System.

Long before this, towards the end of the nineteenth century, an Assamese movement had emerged in Assam. Leaders of the Assamese community sought to establish Assamese as the medium of instruction in schools and colleges. There is evidence that the British government enthusiastically supported these efforts.

Assamese is by no means a recently developed language. Assamese prose had developed long before Bengali prose. It is a rich and mature language. There were historical connections between modern Assamese and Bengali, sustained by social interaction between the two regions. Under British rule, however, competition and rivalry emerged between the two provinces, giving rise to tensions. After 1920, this regional conflict gradually assumed communal and racially discriminatory characteristics. How this transformation occurred deserves closer examination.

Bengal and Assam were neighbouring provinces. Bengal was densely populated, a region that economists and business interests would later describe as possessing an almost unlimited supply of labour, meaning cheap labour. Assam, on the other hand, was regarded as a land-rich province. There was no shortage of uncultivated land in Assam.

The British government in India assumed that the movement of labour and access to land between the two provinces was a natural development. One province had land, while the other had workers. Together, Assam and Bengal could form an ideal combination.

Moreover, for seven years, from 1905 to 1911, the two regions were administered as a single province. Dhaka, in Eastern Bengal, became the capital of this new province. It was considered ‘natural’ that Assam’s middle classes would move to the towns and commercial centres of Eastern Bengal, while peasants from Eastern Bengal would migrate to the uncultivated lands of the Surma and Brahmaputra valleys, cultivate them and increase food production. The only factors regarded as unnatural and regrettable were differences of language, religion and class.

It was the Muslim identity of the Bengali peasants who migrated to Assam that proved to be their misfortune. This gave the Assamese nationalist movement a racial and communal character. After 1920, extremist nationalist organisations such as the Asom Jatiya Mahasabha emerged under the leadership of intellectuals including Ambikagiri Raichoudhury.

III

The struggle of Bengali Muslim peasants against the Line System introduced by the Assam government began for understandable reasons. They were simply demanding the rights of ordinary citizens. Initially, the movement was weak. A division persisted between Bengali Muslims and Assamese Muslims. Many members of the province’s Muslim elite did not look favourably upon the Bengali Muslims from Eastern Bengal, whom they regarded as uncultured or only partially cultured. They disparagingly referred to the newcomers as ‘Mymensinghias’ and ‘Bangals’. Nor did they wholeheartedly welcome the expansion of settlements by these Bengali peasants. The issue involved both ethnic prejudice and class prejudice. For Assamese Hindu society, overcoming hostility towards the Bengali language was no easy task, just as it was difficult for Bengali Hindus living in Assam to overcome their hostility towards Islam. The slogan ‘Bangal Kheda’ (Drive Out the Bengalis) emerged somewhat later. This fascistic movement was a product of the Assamese Hindu reaction. Assamese Muslim society, however, did not fight on behalf of the Bengali Muslim migrants either.

Maulana Bhashani began settling in Goalpara district in the Brahmaputra Valley around 1928. From the very beginning, he mobilised new forces for the movement demanding the abolition of the Line System and opposing the eviction of Bengali migrant peasants under the campaign known as Bangal Kheda. He transformed the numerical strength of the peasantry into a formidable collective force. With the support of these peasants, Maulana Bhashani was elected a member of the Assam Provincial Legislative Assembly, the equivalent of a member of parliament today.

Having been expelled from Bengal for political reasons, he was, in a sense, compelled to enter the political battlefield of Assam. Living among the Bengali Muslim migrants there, he became involved in their movement. How did this happen? Saiful Islam recorded an account in Maulana Bhashani’s own words that offers an answer. He writes:

‘In 1929, he established his right to permanent residence in Assam by building a hut at Char Bhashan (Ghaghamari) for one taka and fourteen annas. The story of how he came to Assam and became involved in politics can be understood from his own account.’

Saiful Islam continues, quoting the Maulana:

‘I did not first come to Assam with any political or social mission. I came as a student of religious knowledge accompanying a pir. My work was to carry the pir’s belongings, run his errands and eat my fill at dawat and ziafat. But when I began mixing with the pir’s followers, I saw that the happiness of the hereafter was very far away, while the suffering of this world was painfully close. Every day was like the torment of hell. Thousands of families and human lives were being devastated by the Line System and Bangal Kheda. So my attention turned away from advancement in the hereafter towards the struggle for survival in this world. As a result, I became involved in the resistance against the Line System and Bangal Kheda. A religious man became a political activist’ (Islam, 2003: 16).
Maulana Bhashani prepares to offer the gayebi janazah in front of Baitul Mukarram as police and EPR personnel attempt to prevent the prayer. Dhaka, December 7, 1968. Photograph: Rashid Talukder.

During the first phase of the movement, he convened a peasant conference at Char Bhashan. At the time, traders in Assam used various kinds of weights and measures in commercial transactions. By manipulating these weights, upper-caste Hindu moneylenders and traders extensively cheated lower-caste Hindus and members of the hill communities. At the conference, Maulana Bhashani demanded an end to fraudulent weighing practices. As a result of Bhashani’s campaign for standardised weights, all weights other than the 80-tola seer were declared illegal in Assam and gradually disappeared from use (Islam, 2003: 16).

Among the other demands raised at the conference was an end to the oppression perpetrated by Raja Prabhat Kumar Barua of Gauripur. Through the Goalpara district administration, the Raja secured an order prohibiting the conference. Maulana Bhashani challenged the prohibition in the Calcutta High Court and won. The conference was successfully held. Abul Kasem Fazlul Huq himself represented the Maulana as his lawyer before the Calcutta High Court. He also attended the conference as its chief guest, quite literally ‘gracing’ the occasion with his presence. By this time, Maulana Bhashani’s reputation had spread to ‘every corner of Assam’. In the general elections held in 1937 under the Government of India Act 1935, he was elected to the Provincial Legislative Assembly.

The mass movement against the Line System now entered the legislative assembly itself. In 1937, the 108-member Assam Provincial Legislative Assembly was divided among ten political groups. The distribution of seats was as follows: ‘Congress 32, Muslim League 4, Assam Valley United People’s Party 8, Progressive Party 12, European Group 13, Independent Party 4, Constitutionalist Party 4, Assam Valley Muslim Group 13, Surma Valley United Muslim Party 17, and one independent member’ (Islam, 2003: 17).

Manowar Ali, an assembly member elected on the ticket of the Surma Valley United Muslim Party, introduced a motion demanding the abolition of the Line System. Abdul Matin Chowdhury of the Muslim League supported the proposal. Maulana Bhashani, an independent member and the leading figure in the movement against the Line System, also participated in the assembly debate. Outside the assembly, he called for a broad-based popular movement to achieve swaraj, or self-rule, bringing together Hindus and Muslims, Bengalis and hill communities alike.

Under the separate electorate system in the 1937 elections, Muslims were allocated 34 of the 108 seats in the Assam Legislative Assembly. Of these, as we have already seen, the Muslim League held only four. When Maulana Bhashani, initially elected as an independent, joined the Muslim League, its strength increased to five seats.

Syed Mohammad Saadulla, a member of Assam’s Muslim elite, also joined the Muslim League, although for a different reason. He was to become the Premier, while Maulana Bhashani was elected president of the Muslim League.

Following Maulana Bhashani’s example, leaders of the Assam Valley Muslim Group and the Surma Valley United Muslim Party gradually joined the Muslim League. Under Bhashani’s leadership, the Assam Provincial Muslim League became the sole political organisation representing Assam’s Muslims. The movement to abolish the Line System thus laid the foundations for the establishment of the Muslim League in Assam.

It must be remembered, however, that Bhashani’s Muslim League did not see eye to eye with the All-India Muslim League on a number of issues. Nor did he agree with Syed Saadulla, the Premier from his own party. Saiful Islam writes:

‘After the fall of the Bordoloi ministry and the formation of the Saadulla ministry, Maulana Bhashani understood that this government would not be able to abolish the Line System or put a complete end to the Bangal Kheda campaign. He also realised that the only difference between Saadulla and Bordoloi was one of the cap and the tiki [the traditional Hindu hair tuft]. The fall of Bordoloi and the return of Saadulla could, at most, lead to some relaxation in the strict enforcement of the Line System’ (Islam, 2003: 21).

Between 1937 and 1947, at least six governments were formed in Assam. The province also experienced a period of Governor’s Rule. Syed Saadulla of the Muslim League and Gopinath Bordoloi of the Congress alternately formed governments. There was, of course, no question of the Bordoloi government abolishing the Line System. But even after repeatedly forming governments, Saadulla did not dare to abolish it either. The Bordoloi government, meanwhile, moved to suppress the movement with even greater severity. During this period, the increasingly militant slogan of ‘Bangal Kheda’ laid the groundwork for ever more extensive eviction campaigns.

Meanwhile, Maulana Bhashani continued his movement against the Line System both inside the assembly and outside it, through conferences, public meetings and political organisations. His differences with Saadulla could no longer be concealed. The All-India Muslim League offered verbal support to the peasant movement led by Bhashani, but it seems unlikely that its leaders genuinely endorsed it.

A single example will help illustrate the situation. On 8 and 9 February 1942, Maulana Bhashani convened the second joint Assam–Bengal Peasants’ Conference at Ghaghamari in Goalpara. He nominated the renowned independence activist Maulana Azad Sobhani as president of the conference. A resolution was adopted declaring that unless the Line System was abolished and Bangal Kheda stopped by 3 March 1942, the movement would adopt a resolution calling for the abolition of landlordism and launch a boycott. Following this declaration, not only the British government and the Congress but also the central leadership of the Muslim League refused to support Bhashani.

At the Muslim League conference held in Barpeta district of Assam on 7 and 8 April 1944, Maulana Bhashani was once again elected president. Another resolution demanding the abolition of the Line System was adopted. Even then, the Saadulla government did not abolish it. During this period, the British government and Congress leaders began portraying the movement against the Line System as a strategy to increase the Muslim population of Assam. Renewed efforts were made to preserve and enforce the system.

Following the February 1944 conference, the Saadulla ministry decided that, in the reserved grazing lands of districts such as Nowgong, Kamrup and Darrang, five bighas of land would be retained for each buffalo and another five bighas for every three cattle, while the remaining land would be distributed among the landless. In certain areas, the boundaries drawn by British officials under the Line System were relaxed or removed. This created opportunities for the Bengali Muslim population to increase in the lower-lying areas of Assam. Taking advantage of what they regarded as an alarming situation, Congress leaders renewed their demands for strict enforcement of the Line System, which had by then weakened somewhat.

On 16 December 1944, an all-party conference was convened at the initiative of Gopinath Bordoloi and Syed Saadulla to resolve disputes over land administration. Among its decisions was a resolution stipulating that only those who had arrived in Assam from outside the province before 1 January 1938, that is, by 31 December 1937, would be considered eligible for land settlement.

Maulana Bhashani and his supporters refused to accept this proposal. They demanded that land be distributed among all those who had arrived in Assam up to 1940. They also insisted that the accursed Line System should eventually be abolished altogether.

Congress leaders, too, disagreed with several resolutions adopted at the all-party conference. They argued that the conference had failed to protect the interests of lower-caste Hindus, hill communities or ‘tribal’ populations, Assamese cattle and buffalo herders, and grass cutters.

In response to these objections from Congress, the Saadulla government attempted to reach a compromise with Congress and other assembly members in March 1945. These efforts culminated in the Tripartite Agreement adopted on 13 July. Under its terms, every Bengali peasant who had arrived after 31 December 1937 was classified as an ‘infiltrator’ and became subject to eviction.

Needless to say, Maulana Bhashani rejected the agreement. He called for a non-cooperation movement and, around May 1946, began a hunger strike demanding the abolition of the Line System, an end to Bangal Kheda and the cessation of campaigns to evict Bengali peasants. He ended his hunger strike after a full 61 days.

Following another peasants’ conference at Mangaldai on 26 June 1946, Maulana Bhashani called his final public meeting in the town of Tezpur in Darrang district. The meeting was scheduled for 10 March 1947. Maulana Bhashani arrived at the gathering in disguise. Immediately after the public meeting, he was arrested.

While he remained in detention, British India was partitioned and the two new states gained independence. He was not released until November 1947. At the time, he was still president of the Assam Provincial Muslim League and a member of the Legislative Assembly. Immediately after his release, arrangements were made to send him to Eastern Bengal, now part of Pakistan, while the eviction campaign continued.

IV

Why did the movement to abolish the Line System fail? Saiful Islam believes that one of the reasons for its failure was the merging of the anti-Line System movement with the ‘communal’ slogan of achieving Pakistan. I reproduce his observations here in full:

‘Despite its enormous scale and intensity, why did the movement to abolish the Line System and suppress Bangal Kheda fail so substantially? A closer examination reveals several reasons: the movement’s inherent weaknesses; its class and regional circumstances; differences between Bhashani and Saadulla in their assessment of and participation in the movement; a shortage of funds; the lack of proper cooperation from the Muslim League high command; the merging of the anti-Line System movement with the communal slogan of achieving Pakistan; Bhashani’s arrest; the deployment of the military to suppress the movement; the partition of the country along communal lines; and the willingness of both the Muslim League and Congress to accept the bait of Partition. Because of these factors, the movement suffered defeat even after coming remarkably close to success’ (Islam, 2003: 48).

I do not possess the scholarly learning necessary to dispute Saiful Islam, but I detected a revealing implication in his criticism.

One question must surely be asked. What role did the Communist Party of India play in the movement to abolish the Line System? This party, too, propagated the views of upper-caste Bengali Hindus. Its own resolutions support this observation. On the question of resolving the problem, the party stated:

‘Bengalis must understand that there is a limit to the amount of cultivable land in Assam. Moreover, the shortage of land in Bengal cannot be remedied by using Assam’s land’ (Islam, 2003: 46–47).

They chose to preserve their social standing rather than uphold their professed principles. In the interest of protecting that standing, the Communist Party’s second resolution was even more remarkable:

‘Experience shows that merely evicting outsiders will not eliminate the danger of forcible occupation of reserved lands’ (Islam, 2003: 47).

The Communist Party’s proposed solution was more remarkable still:

‘The eviction campaign and the illegal, forcible occupation of land must be stopped immediately.’

What more can we possibly add at this point? Let us simply say, Alhamdulillah!

By now, the Communist Party’s straightforward position provides a satisfactory answer to the question of why the movement to abolish the Line System failed. Saiful Islam, an enthusiastic admirer of this position, writes:

‘On 3 May 1947, during a session of the Bengal Provincial Legislative Assembly, Nur Ahmed introduced a private member’s motion urging the central government to abolish the Line System and put an end to the Bangal Kheda campaign. The motion provoked a heated debate between the government and opposition members in the assembly.

‘Amid the exchanges between the Muslim League and Congress, Communist Party member Comrade Jyoti Basu expressed his opinion. He argued that it was deeply shameful that Bengal, instead of providing food for its own children, was pushing them into other regions and provinces. The source of the problem lay in Bengal’s land system. The problem should be resolved by transforming the system of landownership and distribution through a successful united struggle to overthrow its creators and protectors: the landlords, moneylenders and the British’ (Islam, 2003: 47–48).

The movement to abolish the Line System failed to secure support even from the Communist Party of India itself, let alone from other political forces.

‘The peasantry is systematically disregarded for the most part by the propaganda put out by the nationalist parties.’ (Fanon, 1990: 47)

Frantz Fanon (1925–1961) participated in Algeria’s struggle for independence. Long before the Liberation War of 1971, the peasants of Bangladesh had experienced much the same thing. A consideration of Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani’s life also compels us to acknowledge the truth of Fanon’s observation. In this brief essay, I shall confine myself to highlighting this particular lesson.

The life of Maulana Bhashani is, in a sense, the story of Bangladesh’s Muslim peasantry, commonly known as Bengali Muslims.

By a stroke of fortune, he remained largely beyond the reach of colonial education. It seems that the corrupting influence of that education could not entirely diminish his extraordinary character. On numerous occasions, he unmasked the principal comprador or collaborating classes, including landlords, the newly wealthy and the middle classes. He began this work long before the Partition of India, in the province of Assam in undivided India. His name remains unforgettable among the leading figures of the struggle for independence achieved in 1947.

Yet Maulana Bhashani’s contribution to the struggle for independence in 1947 was, in one way or another, erased from the histories written in subsequent decades. This was true not only in the new India but also in the newly established Pakistan. Indeed, apart from a handful of scattered essays, his achievements have remained largely unknown to the wider public to this day.

In this essay, I shall offer only a brief account of Maulana Bhashani’s life, particularly his political career, which began in the province of Assam in undivided India. A comprehensive examination of all its dimensions lies beyond the scope of my knowledge.

I

In 1971, faced with attacks by the Pakistani military, Maulana Bhashani sought refuge in India. Among those who accompanied him was Saiful Islam, a left-wing political activist from the Pabna–Sirajganj region. Indeed, during their wartime exile, he also served as the Maulana’s personal assistant. In 1987, he published some of his recollections and experiences in a volume entitled Swadhinata Bhashani Bharat (Independence, Bhashani and India). About a decade and a half later, around 2002, he published another booklet with the rather cumbersome title Assam O Maulana Bhashani Ebong Line Protha-Bangalkheda (Assam, Maulana Bhashani, the Line System and the Expulsion of Bengalis). This booklet, too, drew upon his experiences of 1971. In it, he attributed many statements directly to Maulana Bhashani, although he did not always specify where or when the Maulana had made them.

As I began reading the booklet, I found myself confronted with a question: Why, and for what reasons, had Maulana Bhashani joined the Pakistan Movement? The answer is not straightforward. Nor does Saiful Islam offer any particularly illuminating answer to this question. I recalled that he, too, belonged to those generally described as leftists in our country. Regrettably, I found that only by carefully considering his various observations might one arrive at something resembling an answer.

Saiful Islam frequently made a point of telling others that, although he enjoyed a good personal relationship with Maulana Bhashani, he did not consider the Maulana’s politics to be correct. At one point in his booklet, Maulana Bhashani O Assam Ebong Line Protha-Bangalkheda, Saiful Islam writes explicitly:

‘I could not agree with him about the involvement of religion in discussion, reasoning, movements, rebellions and revolutions. It was for this reason that, despite having a good personal relationship with Maulana Bhashani, I could not remain politically associated with him’ (Islam, 2003: 25).

Now, in 1971, while Bangladesh’s Liberation War was under way, Saiful Islam asked Maulana Bhashani, as they sat on the soil of Bhashan Char in Assam: ‘Why did you transform the non-communal movement against the Line System in Assam into the communal Pakistan Movement?’ In response, Maulana Bhashani invoked the egalitarian and other positive dimensions of religion.

Saiful Islam had his own convictions. Why would he listen to arguments about religion? The problem lay within his own assumptions. Even before posing the question, he already knew what he expected the answer to be. He had taken it for granted that ‘Pakistan’ was a ‘communal’ phenomenon, or merely another name for communalism. He had no real interest in discovering whether there was anything more to it.

It is true that he did not receive the answer he had hoped for. Yet another kind of answer presented itself to him through an actual event. He failed, however, to recognise that the event itself contained an answer to his question. The Pakistan Movement was not merely a communal movement; it was also a form of national movement.

An examination of the experience of the broad-based popular movement organised under Maulana Bhashani’s leadership to abolish the Line System, introduced by the British colonial government to restrict the settlement of Bengali Muslim peasants in Assam, would likewise demonstrate that the parties leading, or claiming to lead, struggles for national independence have consistently been reluctant to recognise peasant movements as either the foundation of, or participants in, national movements.

Saiful Islam recounts that, at one point during their stay in a refugee camp in India in 1971, Maulana Bhashani expressed a personal wish. He wanted to meet his disciples one last time. There was only one way to bring thousands of his disciples together: to organise an urs, a religious gathering.

According to Saiful Islam’s account, arrangements were made to hold the urs at Bhashan Char. Throughout the night, the disciples engaged in zikr and other devotional recitations. The following day, a vast public gathering took place, with Maulana Bhashani as its sole speaker. Addressing the assembled disciples, followers and members of the wider public, he described the appalling acts of irreligion committed by the Pakistanis in the name of religion. At the same time, he made a point of emphasising the secular character of Bangladesh’s national struggle, that is, its universal appeal.

I have summarised Saiful Islam’s testimony above in my own customary language. I shall now reproduce his observations in his own words:

‘I came to understand that Muslims in India were not supportive of Bangladesh’s struggle for independence, both from my travels through Calcutta, Cooch Behar, Delhi, Dehradun, Ajmer and other places, and from my experiences in Assam. But during Maulana Bhashani’s speech, as I moved around the public gathering, listening to conversations among his disciples of different ages, I repeatedly heard one sentiment expressed: “Huzur wanted Pakistan, so we voted for Pakistan. Now that he no longer wants Pakistan, there must be some deeper wisdom in this.” After the public meeting, I saw that the people departed with an anti-Pakistan outlook’ (Islam, 2003: 25).

Everyone knows that Maulana Bhashani’s original name was Abdul Hamid Khan. Where did this name come from? Those familiar with what is known as the ‘Bengali Muslim mind’ will know that he was named after the Ottoman Sultan Abdul Hamid II, whom Bengali Muslims regarded as the Caliph of Islam. We cannot say with certainty whether Maulana Bhashani was born in 1880 or 1885. We can, however, say that our Abdul Hamid’s life began during the reign of the Ottoman Sultan-Caliph Abdul Hamid II (1876–1909). As for the name by which he became famous throughout the world, ‘Bhashani’, he acquired it from Bhashan Char in Goalpara district of Assam. He was indebted to Assam not merely for the name ‘Bhashani’, but also for his life, youth, wealth and honour. Who, in principle, can be regarded as the true leader of Bengali Muslims? Before any other name comes to mind, there is that of Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani.

This is no small matter. Around the time of his birth, poor peasants from northern Bengal had begun migrating to Assam, particularly the Brahmaputra Valley, where they cultivated previously uncultivated land and established new settlements. This migration was directly connected to British colonial rule. Of those who embarked upon this arduous and hazardous undertaking with the encouragement of the British ruling authorities, the overwhelming majority, an estimated 85 per cent, were Muslims from eastern Bengal.

Even after the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam was abolished in 1911, the Muslim-majority district of Sylhet remained part of Assam. As everyone knows, the whole of Sylhet district remained within Assam until 1947. Karimganj subdivision remains in Assam to this day.

Assam’s long-established Assamese Muslim community constituted a minority. This was the famous Line System.

Long before this, towards the end of the nineteenth century, an Assamese movement had emerged in Assam. Leaders of the Assamese community sought to establish Assamese as the medium of instruction in schools and colleges. There is evidence that the British government enthusiastically supported these efforts.

Assamese is by no means a recently developed language. Assamese prose had developed long before Bengali prose. It is a rich and mature language. There were historical connections between modern Assamese and Bengali, sustained by social interaction between the two regions. Under British rule, however, competition and rivalry emerged between the two provinces, giving rise to tensions. After 1920, this regional conflict gradually assumed communal and racially discriminatory characteristics. How this transformation occurred deserves closer examination.

Bengal and Assam were neighbouring provinces. Bengal was densely populated, a region that economists and business interests would later describe as possessing an almost unlimited supply of labour, meaning cheap labour. Assam, on the other hand, was regarded as a land-rich province. There was no shortage of uncultivated land in Assam.

The British government in India assumed that the movement of labour and access to land between the two provinces was a natural development. One province had land, while the other had workers. Together, Assam and Bengal could form an ideal combination.

Moreover, for seven years, from 1905 to 1911, the two regions were administered as a single province. Dhaka, in Eastern Bengal, became the capital of this new province. The only factors regarded as unnatural and regrettable were differences of language, religion and class.

It was the Muslim identity of the Bengali peasants who migrated to Assam that proved to be their misfortune. This gave the Assamese nationalist movement a racial and communal character. After 1920, extremist nationalist organisations such as the Asom Jatiya Mahasabha emerged under the leadership of intellectuals including Ambikagiri Raichoudhury.

Every day was like the torment of hell. Thousands of families and human lives were being devastated by the Line System and Bangal Kheda. So my attention turned away from advancement in the hereafter towards the struggle for survival in this world. As a result, I became involved in the resistance against the Line System and Bangal Kheda. A religious man became a political activist’ (Islam, 2003: 16).

He called for a non-cooperation movement and, around May 1946, began a hunger strike demanding the abolition of the Line System, an end to Bangal Kheda and the cessation of campaigns to evict Bengali peasants. He ended his hunger strike after a full 61 days.

Following another peasants’ conference at Mangaldai on 26 June 1946, Maulana Bhashani called his final public meeting in the town of Tezpur in Darrang district. The meeting was scheduled for 10 March 1947. Maulana Bhashani arrived at the gathering in disguise. Immediately after the public meeting, he was arrested.

While he remained in detention, British India was partitioned and the two new states gained independence. He was not released until November 1947. At the time, he was still president of the Assam Provincial Muslim League and a member of the Legislative Assembly. Immediately after his release, arrangements were made to send him to Eastern Bengal, now part of Pakistan, while the eviction campaign continued.

IV

Why did the movement to abolish the Line System fail? Saiful Islam believes that one of the reasons for its failure was the merging of the anti-Line System movement with the ‘communal’ slogan of achieving Pakistan. I reproduce his observations here in full:

‘Despite its enormous scale and intensity, why did the movement to abolish the Line System and suppress Bangal Kheda fail so substantially? A closer examination reveals several reasons: the movement’s inherent weaknesses; its class and regional circumstances; differences between Bhashani and Saadulla in their assessment of and participation in the movement; a shortage of funds; the lack of proper cooperation from the Muslim League high command; the merging of the anti-Line System movement with the communal slogan of achieving Pakistan; Bhashani’s arrest; the deployment of the military to suppress the movement; the partition of the country along communal lines; and the willingness of both the Muslim League and Congress to accept the bait of Partition. Because of these factors, the movement suffered defeat even after coming remarkably close to success’ (Islam, 2003: 48).

I do not possess the scholarly learning necessary to dispute Saiful Islam, but I detected a revealing implication in his criticism.

One question must surely be asked. What role did the Communist Party of India play in the movement to abolish the Line System? This party, too, propagated the views of upper-caste Bengali Hindus. Its own resolutions support this observation. On the question of resolving the problem, the party stated:

‘Bengalis must understand that there is a limit to the amount of cultivable land in Assam. Moreover, the shortage of land in Bengal cannot be remedied by using Assam’s land’ (Islam, 2003: 46–47).

They chose to preserve their social standing rather than uphold their professed principles. In the interest of protecting that standing, the Communist Party’s second resolution was even more remarkable:

‘Experience shows that merely evicting outsiders will not eliminate the danger of forcible occupation of reserved lands’ (Islam, 2003: 47).

The Communist Party’s proposed solution was more remarkable still:

‘The eviction campaign and the illegal, forcible occupation of land must be stopped immediately.’

What more can we possibly add at this point? Let us simply say, Alhamdulillah!

By now, the Communist Party’s straightforward position provides a satisfactory answer to the question of why the movement to abolish the Line System failed. Saiful Islam, an enthusiastic admirer of this position, writes:

‘On 3 May 1947, during a session of the Bengal Provincial Legislative Assembly, Nur Ahmed introduced a private member’s motion urging the central government to abolish the Line System and put an end to the Bangal Kheda campaign. The motion provoked a heated debate between the government and opposition members in the assembly.

‘Amid the exchanges between the Muslim League and Congress, Communist Party member Comrade Jyoti Basu expressed his opinion. He argued that it was deeply shameful that Bengal, instead of providing food for its own children, was pushing them into other regions and provinces. The source of the problem lay in Bengal’s land system. The problem should be resolved by transforming the system of landownership and distribution through a successful united struggle to overthrow its creators and protectors: the landlords, moneylenders and the British’ (Islam, 2003: 47–48).

The movement to abolish the Line System failed to secure support even from the Communist Party of India itself, let alone from other political forces.

Dr Salimullah Khan is a professor in the Department of History and Philosophy, School of Humanities and Social Sciences, at North South University.

Translated by Samia Huda.

References

1. Fanon, Frantz (1990). The Wretched of the Earth. Translated by C. Farrington. Reprint. London: Penguin Books.

2. Islam, Saiful (2003). Assam O Maulana Bhashani Ebong Line Protha-Bangal Kheda [Assam, Maulana Bhashani, the Line System and Bangal Kheda]. Third edition. Dhaka: Bortoman Somoy.

item.title: The Daily Star – What the world can learn from Bangladesh's climate innovations
item.description:
Bangladesh is often portrayed as a country threatened by climate change. Yet its achievements in disaster preparedness, community innovation and climate adaptation offer valuable lessons for the world.

When the world discusses Bangladesh and climate change, familiar images dominate: flooded villages, damaged homes, displaced families and communities struggling against rising waters. These realities deserve international attention. Yet they tell only half the story.

Beyond the headlines, Bangladesh is developing something equally important: practical knowledge about adapting to a changing climate.

From floating agriculture to community-based disaster preparedness, the country demonstrates that climate innovation does not always begin in sophisticated laboratories or wealthy economies. Sometimes, it begins with farmers, local communities and institutions determined to protect their livelihoods.

Bangladesh should therefore be recognised not only as a climate-vulnerable nation but also as a source of climate solutions.

Its achievements in disaster preparedness illustrate this potential.

At an international climate meeting in November 2026, Bangladesh's environment ministry highlighted the development of more than 4,200 cyclone shelters and an early-warning network involving over 76,000 volunteers.

These investments have strengthened disaster preparedness, demonstrating that effective adaptation depends not simply on technology but also on public institutions, community participation and sustained investment.

Innovation is also emerging from agriculture.

In flood-prone communities, farmers have developed floating gardens that allow vegetables to grow on beds constructed from organic materials. These systems help maintain food production when conventional farmland becomes submerged.

The United Nations Development Programme has documented innovations involving salt-tolerant crops, integrated farming and climate-resilient livelihoods in coastal Bangladesh.

These practices may appear modest compared with large-scale technological investments. Yet their significance lies in their affordability, adaptability and reliance on local knowledge.
A solar-powered irrigation system supplies water to farmland in Nizpara village of Dinajpur’s Birganj upazila, where electricity remains unavailable. Such renewable energy solutions can help farmers sustain agricultural production while reducing dependence on conventional energy sources. Photo: Kongkon Karmaker

Renewable energy offers additional possibilities.

An Asian Development Bank assessment published in August 2026 documented a solar irrigation initiative involving 641 pumps, with 357 sites integrated into the electricity grid.

The project demonstrated how farmers could reduce their dependence on conventional energy while generating additional income by supplying surplus electricity to the grid.

However, financing and implementation challenges also revealed why promising innovations require effective institutions and sustainable business models.

Bangladesh's experience offers lessons beyond its borders.

Across South and Southeast Asia, countries including India, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam face increasing risks from floods, extreme heat and coastal erosion.

Although circumstances differ, these countries could benefit from exchanging knowledge on community preparedness, climate-resilient agriculture and locally appropriate technologies.

Bangladesh could contribute to this regional exchange while learning from advances in renewable energy, digital infrastructure and climate finance elsewhere.

Nevertheless, innovation alone cannot overcome the scale of the climate challenge.

A 2025 World Bank assessment found that households and businesses across South Asia were already adapting, but many relied on basic solutions because of limited financing and infrastructure.

The report emphasised the need for stronger early-warning systems, accessible credit, insurance and climate-resilient public investment.

Bangladesh has taken steps towards addressing these challenges.

In February 2026, the government introduced its National Framework and Action Plan for Locally Led Adaptation, designed to strengthen community participation and connect national climate policies with local implementation.

The initiative recognises a fundamental principle: communities facing climate risks should help determine how adaptation resources are used.
Farmers cultivate vegetables on floating beds made from water hyacinths and vines in Madhugram, Dumuria upazila, Khulna. This traditional farming method offers a low-cost, climate-resilient way to sustain food production and livelihoods in waterlogged areas. Photo: Habibur Rahman

Three priorities deserve attention.

First, universities, research institutions and businesses should collaborate to transform successful community practices into affordable, scalable technologies.

Second, climate finance must reach local governments, farmers and small enterprises more effectively. Promising innovations cannot expand without reliable funding and technical support.

Third, Bangladesh should strengthen international partnerships that enable its adaptation knowledge to inform development strategies elsewhere.

Importantly, recognising Bangladesh's achievements must not diminish its legitimate need for international climate finance.

At an international meeting in November 2026, Bangladesh's environment ministry estimated annual adaptation needs at approximately US$8.5 billion, against available financing of around US$4 billion.

Innovation and international responsibility must advance together.

Bangladesh's climate future remains challenging. But its experience demonstrates that vulnerability and innovation are not mutually exclusive.

The world should continue supporting Bangladesh in confronting climate risks. It should also pay closer attention to what Bangladesh can teach.

The next breakthrough in climate resilience may not come from the country with the greatest financial resources. It may come from communities that have learned, through necessity and determination, how to turn vulnerability into innovation.

Abd. Rahim Romle is an associate professor and deputy dean at the Ghazali Shafie Graduate School of Government, Universiti Utara Malaysia, Malaysia.

Ainur Rabiyatul Abd. Rahim is a Master of Teaching English as a Second Language (TESL) candidate at Universiti Putra Malaysia, Malaysia.

item.title: The Daily Star – The lonely worlds of Syed Waliullah’s fiction
item.description:
Syed Waliullah was a novelist, a short-story writer and a playwright. Though he was not a prolific writer – he has only three novels, four plays and two short-story collections to his credit – he is recognised as one of the foremost modern writers in Bangla literature, with a Bangla Academy Award to his name. This essay will discuss his fiction, in Bangla as well as in English.

His two volumes of short stories, Nayanchara (1945) and Dui Teer O Anyanya Galpa (1965), contain a total of 17 stories. However, his total number of stories may be around 50. Syed Shamsul Haq attributes about 25 short stories to Syed Waliullah. Syed Waliullah: Galpa Samagra (Jonaki Prakashani, 2021) reveals that he had 32 published stories which he did not anthologise. Ahmed Mostofa Kamal, in Syed Waliullah: Shrestha Galpa (Bishwa Sahitya Kendra, 2008), has included nine stories which were not anthologised by the writer himself. Kamal believes that perhaps Waliullah was too busy or thought the stories did not fit in with the other stories in the anthology.

Waliullah’s correspondence with Anne-Marie Thibaud – who would soon become his wife – suggests a possible reason why another short-story anthology did not soon follow Nayanchara. In a letter dated 24 November 1954, Waliullah tells Anne-Marie about a volume of short stories he was putting together. According to him, the manuscript was ready for the press: “I have collected most of them. I am now busy retouching them which I find absolutely necessary. . . . Though you will not understand the language, I will send you a proofcopy containing these titles. You can at least say if they look good” (in Anne-Marie Waliullah’s Waliullah: My Husband as I Knew Him, Nymphea, 2022).
 
Syed Waliullah in Paris, January 1965.

Waliullah believed that the manuscript would be ready for the press by Friday – that is, two days later. He had been planning to write a novel in English, but he told Anne-Marie that work on the book had to be suspended for the Bangla short-story collection. He also had to write a play of about 12,000 words for PEN. No one knows what happened to this collection of short stories, as his second short-story anthology appeared almost ten years later. The English novel he was planning was perhaps suspended permanently.

From his posting in Karachi in 1951 to his subsequent postings in Jakarta, London and Bonn, and finally to Paris in 1961, where he lived until his death in 1971, Waliullah lived away from his homeland and his Bangla-speaking milieu. However, he never forgot the land where he had spent his childhood and youth. Most of his short stories, whether in Bangla or English, are set in Bengal, though a few are set on board a boat or a ship, some in a place that could be anywhere on earth, and one in an undetermined space between two countries. Lal Salu (1948), as well as the two Bangla novels he wrote in Europe – Chander Amabasya (1963) and Kando Nadi Kando (1966) – are set in Bengal.

Almost all of Waliullah’s fiction has a sad ending. Perhaps losing his mother when he was very young left a void in Waliullah’s life, which is reflected in much of his fiction. As Anne-Marie notes in Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him, “This constant shift of places, which means he most likely could not make close school friends, together with the loss of his mother at the age of eight, partly explains his reserved character, his aloofness and some of his rootlessness.”
 
Cover of Syed Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him by Anne-Marie Waliullah (Nymphea, 2022), a personal account of the celebrated Bengali novelist’s life and literary journey.

His father’s second marriage must also have affected him. Though later in life Waliullah always visited his half-brothers, half-sisters, stepmother and step-aunt when he returned to his homeland, they could not fill the void in his life. Moreover, Waliullah’s relationship with his father was not a close one. Syed Ahmedullah could not understand his artistic son. His step-aunt relates how upset his father was when he came upon his son drawing instead of studying. He tore up the painting and pulled his son up by his hair. Waliullah quietly said, “I’ll have to cut my hair to go on painting.” The relationship between son and father may be seen replicated in different ways in his fiction, most particularly in the relationship between Mohammad Mustafa and his father in Kando Nadi Kando. Thanks to the nature of his father’s job, Waliullah got to see the small mofussil towns of Bengal, but the unhappy relationship between father and son, who showed no keenness to follow in his father’s footsteps and become a civil servant, is revealed in his fiction, as well as in what we learn from his letters to his wife and other sources.

The tone of nostalgia and gloom, perhaps what may be called an existential despair, is present in many of his stories, whether written in Bangla or English. Stories like “No Enemy” and “Cargo” – both written in English and later translated by Waliullah into Bangla – as well as “Mrityuyatra” (The Death March) reveal an existential despair, as do his later novels Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando.

Waliullah wrote only three novels in Bangla: Lal Salu (transcreated as Tree Without Roots, 1967), Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando. Lal Salu, referring to the red cloth used to cover shrines, is Syed Waliullah’s first and most famous novel. Initially published by Comrade Publishers in Calcutta, Lal Salu was subsequently published in Dhaka, East Pakistan, and continues to be published in Bangladesh.
 
The cover of the first edition of Syed Waliullah’s debut novel, Lal Salu (1948), designed by Zainul Abedin.

Lal Salu narrates the story of Majeed, who finds a neglected shrine and pretends that it is the resting place of a famous Muslim saint. Appointing himself as its guardian, he preys upon the simple villagers. He marries Rahima, a childless widow. After some years of a childless marriage, he takes a second wife, a young girl named Jamila. Unlike the docile Rahima, Jamila has a mind of her own. One day, Majeed decides to punish her and forces her to spend the night alone in the shrine. However, that night there is a violent hailstorm. When Majeed goes to the shrine to see how Jamila is, he finds her unconscious. Alarmed, he takes her to their hut and leaves her with Rahima. He then sets off to check what damage the hailstorm has caused to his crops. On the way, villagers come to him, lamenting their losses. Majeed tells them not to lose faith in God. The Bangla novel ends here, with Majeed and the villagers looking at the fields destroyed by the hail.

In 1963, Anne-Marie Thibaud’s French translation of the book, L’arbre sans racine, was published. Four years later, an English translation of the novel appeared as Tree Without Roots, with the title translated from the French. Four translators were credited: Anne-Marie Thibaud, Qaiser Saeed, Jeffrey Gibian and Malik Khayyam. However, in Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him, Anne-Marie describes how she had translated the book, as well as Chander Amabasya, from Waliullah’s own English translation.
 
The cover of Tree Without Roots (1967), Syed Waliullah’s English transcreation of Lal Salu, the first of his three Bangla novels.

Waliullah could not resist correcting or improving what he had written earlier. Even published pieces are marked by corrections or changes. The English translation that he had prepared of Lal Salu, so that his wife could translate it into French, was done more than a decade after he had written the novel. Apart from the change in the title, there are several other changes. Perhaps the most striking ones are in the opening and final chapters. The poverty of the land is described in vivid language: “There are too many of them on this land, this piece of raped and ravaged land which yields no more. They know it, but what can they do? Every inch of it is ploughed and sown.”

The most significant deviations of Tree Without Roots from the Bangla original are the added chapters at the end, which make Majeed a more complex character than in Lal Salu. The Damra, a quiet river which was thought to be dying, has flooded, and Majeed realises that the river has become so powerful that, at any moment, it could break its high bank and flood his hut and the shrine. He cannot leave the shrine which he has created, but at least he can save his wives. Accompanied by Rahima and carrying Jamila in his arms, he takes them to his friend Khaleque’s house and asks him to look after them. Leaving them there, he returns through the floodwaters to the shrine: “A thin, haggard man, with sunken, utterly expressionless eyes, his sparse beard as pale as the dawn, a frail human speck standing alone on the edge of a vast expanse of water that merged into the infinite vastness of the sky.”

Syed Waliullah’s second novel, Chander Amabasya, opens with the description of a moonlit scene in a bamboo grove. Aref Ali, a young teacher who happens to be there, discovers the half-naked dead body of a young woman. When he emerges from the bamboo grove, he notices a man whom he recognises as Qadir, the younger brother of Dada Sahib, the elderly man who has hired him. Though Aref Ali recognises Qadir, he cannot connect the man to the dead woman.
 
The cover of Chander Amabasya, Syed Waliullah’s second novel. It opens in a moonlit bamboo grove, where a young teacher’s discovery draws him into a moral dilemma.

Later, Qadir asks for Aref Ali’s help in burying the woman. Aref Ali thinks that the murder was an accident and that Qadir was in love with the young woman. He believes that Qadir wanted to hide the woman’s body because he was in love with her and did not want her half-naked body to be seen by people. However, when Aref Ali realises that Qadir had never loved the woman, he decides that it is his moral duty to tell Dada Sahib, his patron, as well as the police.

He does so. However, the police do not seem to believe his story. He finds himself being accused of the murder. Apart from him, there is no witness, and he is told that he has been seen committing the murder. Aref Ali ponders over the death of the young woman and thinks that someone has to be punished for the crime. Even, perhaps, he himself. As in the later Kando Nadi Kando, Chander Amabasya also asks the same moral question: How far is a person responsible for an act committed by someone else?

Syed Waliullah’s Kando Nadi Kando, translated by Osman Jamal as Cry, River, Cry (2015), tells two parallel stories: one of a dying river, Barkal, and the other of Muhammad Mustafa, a young magistrate in charge of administering a small town. There are two narrators: Tabarak Bhuiyan and an unnamed narrator, the cousin of Muhammad Mustafa. Bhuiyan was a booking clerk at the steamer station when Mustafa became a magistrate.

One day, the steamer station is dismantled, an acknowledgement that the river is dying. That same night, Sakina Khatun, the daughter of Mokhtar Moslehuddin, hears a strange cry. Sakina says, “The river is crying. The river Barkal is crying.” Believing that if they give gifts to the river, it will not die, the townspeople throw whatever they can into the river: a slaughtered calf, pots, pans, clothes, rice, pulses, gold and silver ornaments.
 
The cover of Syed Waliullah’s Kando Nadi Kando, translated into English by Osman Jamal as Cry, River, Cry in 2015.

Mustafa is supposed to board the steamer on the day it does not arrive. When Mustafa returns home, he hears that his cousin, Khodija, has committed suicide. As children, Mustafa and Khodija had been pledged to each other by his father. When Khodija learnt that he was getting married to someone else, she drowned herself in the small pond behind the house. Mustafa is tormented by the thought that she committed suicide because of him, and wonders how far human beings are responsible for the actions of others. Finally, one morning, the household awakes to find that Mustafa has hanged himself from a tamarind tree, his eyes looking towards the algae-covered, stagnant pond where Khodija had drowned herself.

In addition to these three novels, Syed Waliullah wrote one English novel, The Ugly Asian, under the pseudonym Abu Sharya. The novel was published posthumously in 2013 by the Bangla Academy.

Waliullah had high hopes that this novel, so different from his Bangla novels, would be accepted by a Western publisher. His letter, dated 5 July 1961, to Macmillan Publishers expressed the hope that “a novel about Asian reaction to the problem dealt with in ‘The Ugly American’ by William J. Lederer and Eugene Burdick may interest many people in the West.” He explained that he was “a Bengali novelist and [enjoyed] some reputation in serious circles.” His Bangla novel had also received an award from “the Bengali Academy of East Pakistan.” However, he wished to publish the English novel under a pseudonym and therefore wanted the correspondence to remain confidential.
 
The cover of How Does One Cook Beans? and Selected Fiction, edited by Niaz Zaman and published by University Press Limited (UPL) on 30 October 2026. Waliullah wrote the unfinished work in English under the pseudonym Abu Sharya.

We do not have Macmillan’s reply.

A political allegory, The Ugly Asian takes place in an imaginary Asian country where there has just been a change of government. However, the new government is as corrupt and hostile to the people as the previous one. Set during the Cold War, the novel explores the relationship between the US and the Asian country, which is attempting to throw off its colonial roots and becomes the setting for America's proxy struggle against Communism.

Though different in language and theme from Waliullah’s other novels, The Ugly Asian, too, has a lonely hero in Professor Ahsan. Professor Ahsan fails, much as Majeed, Aref Ali and Muhammad Mustafa – the protagonists of his Bangla novels – fail. Unlike them, however, he is a political figure and, through him, Waliullah voices his opinions on American politics and how South Asian countries are affected. Ahsan tells an American named Johnson, who is on a “fact-finding mission”, that even a small nation must be left to itself to decide what it wants. “Go and defend your own shores but not mine. I do not want you to defend anything of mine because I know that you are not defending me but yourself. I do not therefore accept you as my defender. If the other side comes to my country to defend itself, I will also ask him to leave my country.” If America really wants to help Asians, it must learn what Asians want. In “An Asian Speaks”, an afterword to The Ugly Asian, there is an imagined dialogue between an Asian peasant and an American who speaks his language fluently. The American tries to convince the Asian that Communism is bad but fails to do so: “The American spoke the man’s language. But the man did not understand what the American meant.”
 
Syed Waliullah and his wife, Anne-Marie Waliullah, in 1955.

As mentioned earlier, Syed Waliullah had also attempted to write a novel in English in 1954. He was at the time posted in East Pakistan, separated from the woman whom he would marry a year later. He was lonely and depressed. In a letter to Anne-Marie, dated 15 October 1954, he told her he was writing “a novel about the life in the villages here but with my individual notes interwoven throughout.” In a later letter to her, dated 5 November 1954, he said, “I feel so uncertain about my future. . . . that is why I am putting so much faith and hope in the book I am writing. I have a feeling if it is accepted by an outside publisher, I might take a bold decision.”

This book was not The Ugly Asian, which is not about villages but about American politics in Asia. Did Syed Waliullah ever write this book? If he had written even a few pages, Anne-Marie would have kept them safe, just as she kept all his published and unpublished writings safe – something their daughter Simine is doing now.

One piece of unfinished English writing which Anne-Marie kept safe was a work very different from his other writings. Written in English, like The Ugly Asian, and, like it, under the pseudonym Abu Sharya, it is very different in tone, setting and theme from that novel. How Does One Cook Beans begins in a South Asian country but then shifts with the narrator to France. It is a humorous piece of writing, reflecting the side of Waliullah that his family and friends saw. Though there is a sort of an ending, it is unfinished. He had started writing it in 1961, but perhaps the demands of life, work and family intervened, and he could not finish it. Instead, he went on to write two other Bangla novels, Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando – both set in his homeland.

Niaz Zaman is a retired academic, writer and translator.
