According to him, the manuscript was ready for the press: “I have collected most of them. I am now busy retouching them which I find absolutely necessary. . . . Though you will not understand the language, I will send you a proofcopy containing these titles. You can at least say if they look good” (in Anne-Marie Waliullah’s Waliullah: My Husband as I Knew Him, Nymphea, 2022).
 
Syed Waliullah in Paris, January 1965.

Waliullah believed that the manuscript would be ready for the press by Friday – that is, two days later. He had been planning to write a novel in English, but he told Anne-Marie that work on the book had to be suspended for the Bangla short-story collection. He also had to write a play of about 12,000 words for PEN. No one knows what happened to this collection of short stories, as his second short-story anthology appeared almost ten years later. The English novel he was planning was perhaps suspended permanently.

From his posting in Karachi in 1951 to his subsequent postings in Jakarta, London and Bonn, and finally to Paris in 1961, where he lived until his death in 1971, Waliullah lived away from his homeland and his Bangla-speaking milieu. However, he never forgot the land where he had spent his childhood and youth. Most of his short stories, whether in Bangla or English, are set in Bengal, though a few are set on board a boat or a ship, some in a place that could be anywhere on earth, and one in an undetermined space between two countries. Lal Salu (1948), as well as the two Bangla novels he wrote in Europe – Chander Amabasya (1963) and Kando Nadi Kando (1966) – are set in Bengal.

Almost all of Waliullah’s fiction has a sad ending. Perhaps losing his mother when he was very young left a void in Waliullah’s life, which is reflected in much of his fiction. As Anne-Marie notes in Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him, “This constant shift of places, which means he most likely could not make close school friends, together with the loss of his mother at the age of eight, partly explains his reserved character, his aloofness and some of his rootlessness.”
 
Cover of Syed Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him by Anne-Marie Waliullah (Nymphea, 2022), a personal account of the celebrated Bengali novelist’s life and literary journey.

His father’s second marriage must also have affected him. Though later in life Waliullah always visited his half-brothers, half-sisters, stepmother and step-aunt when he returned to his homeland, they could not fill the void in his life. Moreover, Waliullah’s relationship with his father was not a close one. Syed Ahmedullah could not understand his artistic son. His step-aunt relates how upset his father was when he came upon his son drawing instead of studying. He tore up the painting and pulled his son up by his hair. Waliullah quietly said, “I’ll have to cut my hair to go on painting.” The relationship between son and father may be seen replicated in different ways in his fiction, most particularly in the relationship between Mohammad Mustafa and his father in Kando Nadi Kando. Thanks to the nature of his father’s job, Waliullah got to see the small mofussil towns of Bengal, but the unhappy relationship between father and son, who showed no keenness to follow in his father’s footsteps and become a civil servant, is revealed in his fiction, as well as in what we learn from his letters to his wife and other sources.

The tone of nostalgia and gloom, perhaps what may be called an existential despair, is present in many of his stories, whether written in Bangla or English. Stories like “No Enemy” and “Cargo” – both written in English and later translated by Waliullah into Bangla – as well as “Mrityuyatra” (The Death March) reveal an existential despair, as do his later novels Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando.

Waliullah wrote only three novels in Bangla: Lal Salu (transcreated as Tree Without Roots, 1967), Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando. Lal Salu, referring to the red cloth used to cover shrines, is Syed Waliullah’s first and most famous novel. Initially published by Comrade Publishers in Calcutta, Lal Salu was subsequently published in Dhaka, East Pakistan, and continues to be published in Bangladesh.
 
The cover of the first edition of Syed Waliullah’s debut novel, Lal Salu (1948), designed by Zainul Abedin.

Lal Salu narrates the story of Majeed, who finds a neglected shrine and pretends that it is the resting place of a famous Muslim saint. Appointing himself as its guardian, he preys upon the simple villagers. He marries Rahima, a childless widow. After some years of a childless marriage, he takes a second wife, a young girl named Jamila. Unlike the docile Rahima, Jamila has a mind of her own. One day, Majeed decides to punish her and forces her to spend the night alone in the shrine. However, that night there is a violent hailstorm. When Majeed goes to the shrine to see how Jamila is, he finds her unconscious. Alarmed, he takes her to their hut and leaves her with Rahima. He then sets off to check what damage the hailstorm has caused to his crops. On the way, villagers come to him, lamenting their losses. Majeed tells them not to lose faith in God. The Bangla novel ends here, with Majeed and the villagers looking at the fields destroyed by the hail.

In 1963, Anne-Marie Thibaud’s French translation of the book, L’arbre sans racine, was published. Four years later, an English translation of the novel appeared as Tree Without Roots, with the title translated from the French. Four translators were credited: Anne-Marie Thibaud, Qaiser Saeed, Jeffrey Gibian and Malik Khayyam. However, in Waliullah: My Husband as I Saw Him, Anne-Marie describes how she had translated the book, as well as Chander Amabasya, from Waliullah’s own English translation.
 
The cover of Tree Without Roots (1967), Syed Waliullah’s English transcreation of Lal Salu, the first of his three Bangla novels.

Waliullah could not resist correcting or improving what he had written earlier. Even published pieces are marked by corrections or changes. The English translation that he had prepared of Lal Salu, so that his wife could translate it into French, was done more than a decade after he had written the novel. Apart from the change in the title, there are several other changes. Perhaps the most striking ones are in the opening and final chapters. The poverty of the land is described in vivid language: “There are too many of them on this land, this piece of raped and ravaged land which yields no more. They know it, but what can they do? Every inch of it is ploughed and sown.”

The most significant deviations of Tree Without Roots from the Bangla original are the added chapters at the end, which make Majeed a more complex character than in Lal Salu. The Damra, a quiet river which was thought to be dying, has flooded, and Majeed realises that the river has become so powerful that, at any moment, it could break its high bank and flood his hut and the shrine. He cannot leave the shrine which he has created, but at least he can save his wives. Accompanied by Rahima and carrying Jamila in his arms, he takes them to his friend Khaleque’s house and asks him to look after them. Leaving them there, he returns through the floodwaters to the shrine: “A thin, haggard man, with sunken, utterly expressionless eyes, his sparse beard as pale as the dawn, a frail human speck standing alone on the edge of a vast expanse of water that merged into the infinite vastness of the sky.”

Syed Waliullah’s second novel, Chander Amabasya, opens with the description of a moonlit scene in a bamboo grove. Aref Ali, a young teacher who happens to be there, discovers the half-naked dead body of a young woman. When he emerges from the bamboo grove, he notices a man whom he recognises as Qadir, the younger brother of Dada Sahib, the elderly man who has hired him. Though Aref Ali recognises Qadir, he cannot connect the man to the dead woman.
 
The cover of Chander Amabasya, Syed Waliullah’s second novel. It opens in a moonlit bamboo grove, where a young teacher’s discovery draws him into a moral dilemma.

Later, Qadir asks for Aref Ali’s help in burying the woman. Aref Ali thinks that the murder was an accident and that Qadir was in love with the young woman. He believes that Qadir wanted to hide the woman’s body because he was in love with her and did not want her half-naked body to be seen by people. However, when Aref Ali realises that Qadir had never loved the woman, he decides that it is his moral duty to tell Dada Sahib, his patron, as well as the police.

He does so. However, the police do not seem to believe his story. He finds himself being accused of the murder. Apart from him, there is no witness, and he is told that he has been seen committing the murder. Aref Ali ponders over the death of the young woman and thinks that someone has to be punished for the crime. Even, perhaps, he himself. As in the later Kando Nadi Kando, Chander Amabasya also asks the same moral question: How far is a person responsible for an act committed by someone else?

Syed Waliullah’s Kando Nadi Kando, translated by Osman Jamal as Cry, River, Cry (2015), tells two parallel stories: one of a dying river, Barkal, and the other of Muhammad Mustafa, a young magistrate in charge of administering a small town. There are two narrators: Tabarak Bhuiyan and an unnamed narrator, the cousin of Muhammad Mustafa. Bhuiyan was a booking clerk at the steamer station when Mustafa became a magistrate.

One day, the steamer station is dismantled, an acknowledgement that the river is dying. That same night, Sakina Khatun, the daughter of Mokhtar Moslehuddin, hears a strange cry. Sakina says, “The river is crying. The river Barkal is crying.” Believing that if they give gifts to the river, it will not die, the townspeople throw whatever they can into the river: a slaughtered calf, pots, pans, clothes, rice, pulses, gold and silver ornaments.
 
The cover of Syed Waliullah’s Kando Nadi Kando, translated into English by Osman Jamal as Cry, River, Cry in 2015.

Mustafa is supposed to board the steamer on the day it does not arrive. When Mustafa returns home, he hears that his cousin, Khodija, has committed suicide. As children, Mustafa and Khodija had been pledged to each other by his father. When Khodija learnt that he was getting married to someone else, she drowned herself in the small pond behind the house. Mustafa is tormented by the thought that she committed suicide because of him, and wonders how far human beings are responsible for the actions of others. Finally, one morning, the household awakes to find that Mustafa has hanged himself from a tamarind tree, his eyes looking towards the algae-covered, stagnant pond where Khodija had drowned herself.

In addition to these three novels, Syed Waliullah wrote one English novel, The Ugly Asian, under the pseudonym Abu Sharya. The novel was published posthumously in 2013 by the Bangla Academy.

Waliullah had high hopes that this novel, so different from his Bangla novels, would be accepted by a Western publisher. His letter, dated 5 July 1961, to Macmillan Publishers expressed the hope that “a novel about Asian reaction to the problem dealt with in ‘The Ugly American’ by William J. Lederer and Eugene Burdick may interest many people in the West.” He explained that he was “a Bengali novelist and [enjoyed] some reputation in serious circles.” His Bangla novel had also received an award from “the Bengali Academy of East Pakistan.” However, he wished to publish the English novel under a pseudonym and therefore wanted the correspondence to remain confidential.
 
The cover of How Does One Cook Beans? and Selected Fiction, edited by Niaz Zaman and published by University Press Limited (UPL) on 30 October 2026. Waliullah wrote the unfinished work in English under the pseudonym Abu Sharya.

We do not have Macmillan’s reply.

A political allegory, The Ugly Asian takes place in an imaginary Asian country where there has just been a change of government. However, the new government is as corrupt and hostile to the people as the previous one. Set during the Cold War, the novel explores the relationship between the US and the Asian country, which is attempting to throw off its colonial roots and becomes the setting for America's proxy struggle against Communism.

Though different in language and theme from Waliullah’s other novels, The Ugly Asian, too, has a lonely hero in Professor Ahsan. Professor Ahsan fails, much as Majeed, Aref Ali and Muhammad Mustafa – the protagonists of his Bangla novels – fail. Unlike them, however, he is a political figure and, through him, Waliullah voices his opinions on American politics and how South Asian countries are affected. Ahsan tells an American named Johnson, who is on a “fact-finding mission”, that even a small nation must be left to itself to decide what it wants. “Go and defend your own shores but not mine. I do not want you to defend anything of mine because I know that you are not defending me but yourself. I do not therefore accept you as my defender. If the other side comes to my country to defend itself, I will also ask him to leave my country.” If America really wants to help Asians, it must learn what Asians want. In “An Asian Speaks”, an afterword to The Ugly Asian, there is an imagined dialogue between an Asian peasant and an American who speaks his language fluently. The American tries to convince the Asian that Communism is bad but fails to do so: “The American spoke the man’s language. But the man did not understand what the American meant.”
 
Syed Waliullah and his wife, Anne-Marie Waliullah, in 1955.

As mentioned earlier, Syed Waliullah had also attempted to write a novel in English in 1954. He was at the time posted in East Pakistan, separated from the woman whom he would marry a year later. He was lonely and depressed. In a letter to Anne-Marie, dated 15 October 1954, he told her he was writing “a novel about the life in the villages here but with my individual notes interwoven throughout.” In a later letter to her, dated 5 November 1954, he said, “I feel so uncertain about my future. . . . that is why I am putting so much faith and hope in the book I am writing. I have a feeling if it is accepted by an outside publisher, I might take a bold decision.”

This book was not The Ugly Asian, which is not about villages but about American politics in Asia. Did Syed Waliullah ever write this book? If he had written even a few pages, Anne-Marie would have kept them safe, just as she kept all his published and unpublished writings safe – something their daughter Simine is doing now.

One piece of unfinished English writing which Anne-Marie kept safe was a work very different from his other writings. Written in English, like The Ugly Asian, and, like it, under the pseudonym Abu Sharya, it is very different in tone, setting and theme from that novel. How Does One Cook Beans begins in a South Asian country but then shifts with the narrator to France. It is a humorous piece of writing, reflecting the side of Waliullah that his family and friends saw. Though there is a sort of an ending, it is unfinished. He had started writing it in 1961, but perhaps the demands of life, work and family intervened, and he could not finish it. Instead, he went on to write two other Bangla novels, Chander Amabasya and Kando Nadi Kando – both set in his homeland.

Niaz Zaman is a retired academic, writer and translator.

item.title: The Daily Star – Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq: Revisiting a complex legacy
item.description: One of the most influential political figures in the history of Bengal, Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq left an enduring legacy through his advocacy for peasant rights, his challenge to entrenched political and economic power, and his role in shaping the politics of colonial and postcolonial Bengal. Yet his political thought, achievements and contradictions deserve renewed attention beyond familiar historical narratives. Through a collection of essays and historical analyses, The Daily Star's Slow Reads revisits his life, political struggles, ideas and legacy, exploring how his vision and actions shaped Bengal's past and continue to resonate in Bangladesh today.

item.title: The Daily Star – Bagh-Mama and beyond: The forgotten world of animals in vintage Bengali advertising
item.description:
The year is 1799. A notice appears in the Calcutta Gazette. Somewhere in Lalbazar, inside the courtyard of an Englishman’s residence, a magnificent tigress from the Sundarbans and her cubs are held in a cage. Citizens are invited to witness the spectacle. The admission fee is a modest eight annas, collected by the keeper of the beasts. One wonders how many curious souls parted with their coins back then to catch a glimpse of the ‘bagh-mama’.

Looking back across the centuries, one can only wish the advertisement had featured a picture of the tiger. Even today, we could have feasted our eyes on it.

The year is 1857. A notice is published in the Sambad Prabhakar by Darogah Brojomohon Roy. A chowkidar from Badamtala police station has captured a ‘Lalmohan’ bird. Should any rightful owner come forward, the bird can be claimed at the station. A modern researcher hazards a guess. The bird likely belonged to some affluent gentleman of contemporary Calcutta. Perhaps, he suggests, the advertisement was placed in the hope of receiving a reward upon its return. Perhaps so. Yet, even here, how thrilled we would have been to behold a picture of ‘Lalmohan-babu’, safely kept in the darogah’s custody!

The year is long gone, yet the practice is familiar. Advertisements for the sale of horses in those days invariably featured woodcut illustrations.

More often than not, these notices were issued by the Calcutta auctioneers Cook & Company. The horse advertisements would meticulously detail how long the animals could endure in battle or whether they possessed the stamina for the racecourse. Atop the notices for horses imported from Australia, a neat little engraving of a horse would sit proudly. Elephants were traded just as readily in this bustling market of majestic beasts. Yet, when an elephant was sold at official government rates, there was no picture to accompany it. One simply had to read the words and imagine its beauty and fine training, much like that old ‘bagh-mama’ or our dear ‘Lalmohan-babu’.
 
A strange-looking tiger in a 1922 rasogolla advertisement, a crudely drawn man fighting a lion on a matchbox, and a remarkably lifelike tiger illustrated by Protul Bandyopadhyay for a gun advertisement in the 1930s.

The year is 1922. A unique advertisement appears in newspapers, featuring the most bizarre drawing of a tiger one could ever encounter. Even John Lawson, the missionary artist of Pashwabali, would surely have smiled at the sight of it. It is not a full-body portrait of the beast, but merely its face. One might playfully remark that the tiger looks precisely like an elderly uncle relaxing in an easy chair. The accompanying copy offers plenty of amusement, too. It boldly claims that these rasogollas are stored in such airtight tins that “even if you open the tin after ten years, you will find them fresh.” Imagine the sheer magnitude of the falsehoods printed in advertisements back then!

I am not here to judge which promotions were sheer fraud and which were not. Nor do I intend to nitpick the artistic flaws of bygone eras. My sole endeavour is to trace the qualitative evolution of animal illustrations in Bengali advertisements across this subcontinent.

Bengalis have gazed upon illustrations of tigers since time immemorial. Their majestic terror runs riot across the pages of Bengali literature. A comprehensive list would have no end. Who has not drawn them? From Haridas Sen and Upendra Kishore Raychowdhury to countless modern artists.

The unforgettable Tuntunir Boi is a treasure trove of vivid imagery: a fox tying a tiger by the tail to make it leap twenty-five yards; a tiger fleeing at the crash of a breaking pot; a tiger dressed as a bridegroom; a tiger tied to a stake, and so many more. These illustrations etched themselves into our minds, driven less by their artistic perfection than by the sheer pull of the tales. We have even beheld Nandalal Bose’s sketch gifted to Satyajit Ray, depicting the tiger whose tail-tip gets scorched in the hearth while trying to steal cooked meat. In Sahajpath, Nandalal once again showed us what a tiger in the wild truly looks like. How much more can one recount?

The long and short of it is simple. One can safely close one's eyes and swear that no one except the artist himself could ever have witnessed a tiger like the one in that advertisement from the Bagbazar sweet company. Consider Rabindranath's famous rhyme about a plump tiger with dark stripes who wanders into a room to eat the bearer, encounters a mirror, and flees in terror at his own reflection, roaring angrily over why his body is covered in black stripes
(“এক ছিল মোটা কেঁদো বাঘ,/ গায়ে তার কালো কালো দাগ।/ বেহারাকে খেতে ঘরে ঢুকে/ আয়নাটা পড়েছে সমুখে।/ এক ছুটে পালালো বেহারা,/ বাঘ দেখে আপন চেহারা।/ গাঁ গাঁ করে ডেকে ওঠে রাগে,/ দেহ কেন ভরা কালো দাগে”).

We also remember the tiger illustration by Nandalal Bose in the book Chitra-Bichitra. That tiger, drawn by Nandalal Bose, is not realistic at all; rather, it is created in the style of our folk art and ancient sculptures, bearing no resemblance to the real tigers we see in zoos. Yet, much like that strange tiger painted on a sweet tin, we have seen many such creatures in folk paintings, in traditional depictions of the Goddess’s mount, in those strange horse-faced lions, or in old sculptures. We know that these pictures were not drawn from life; they came from the pure imagination of the artists.

Sometimes I wonder: do today's teenagers read Tuntunir Golpo anymore? I can hardly tell. From what I gather from a couple of them, once the spell of animation wears off, they are far more clued up about Puma’s leaping black panther logo or Sabyasachi’s fashion label featuring a tiger on a black belt. And they have every right to be.

Yet, we are not speaking of the present day. We are talking about tigers sketched in advertisements a hundred or a hundred and fifty years ago. Once upon a time, one could catch a glimpse of their glorious faces on matchboxes. Perhaps one still can. The enduring appeal of the tiger as a brand is widely known. Even so, the finest and most accurately drawn tiger in Bengali advertising, from a time when the majestic beast itself had yet to face the present threat of extinction, was to be found somewhere else entirely.

In the days before tiger hunting was banned by law, a Bengali advertisement regularly appeared in the 1930s, featuring a tiger emerging from the bushes. The drawing was absolutely flawless.

Narsingha Chand & Company, the “renowned gun merchants”, claimed to offer the ultimate, infallible weapon for a successful hunt. The shop's address was ‘56 Old China Bazar Street’. Catalogues were also sent out “upon writing a letter”. It is quite likely that the catalogue featured that very same picture of the tiger. The Narsingha brothers surely meant to suggest that if one must buy a gun, the ultimate quarry for a Bengali ought to be the ‘Royal Bengal Tiger’! The artist had signed the illustration with the English initials ‘P.B.’ It was easy enough to figure out that this was Protul Bandyopadhyay, born in the village of Hridaypur in Nadia. Trained at the Art College and under Abanindranath, his illustrations, especially those for children, have secured a permanent place in the history of Bengali art. But how many people know that he also drew for advertisements?

I once came across another example in a 1946 issue of Art in Industry, a magazine published in Calcutta by the Indian Institute of Art in Industry. There, an ordinary man from the subcontinent, dressed in a dhoti, fatua and turban, is seen riding on the back of a leaping tiger. The tiger, in turn, casts a sideways glance at the viewer. Accompanying the artwork was that intensely familiar and formidable catchphrase, rendered in lettering: “He who rides a tiger cannot dismount.”

It is a cartoon-like illustration. The characters are brought to life through simple, fluid lines. The artwork is dominated primarily by shades of orange and black, which harmonise with the natural colours of a tiger’s coat. Additionally, a bright red turban adorns the character’s head. The tiger's leaping posture and its fierce, swift expression lend the picture a sense of dynamism. Yet, it is also profoundly thought-provoking. There is no signature of the artist on this one. Spotting a signature on an advertising illustration is a rare stroke of good fortune indeed!
 
The portrayal of tigers in Bengali advertisements evolved over time, reflecting changing artistic styles, techniques and approaches to commercial illustration.

Though not quite as brilliantly executed, another advertisement from much later, in 1948, for Tiger Brand paper, showed a ‘bagh-mama’ roaring as it was about to step out of a halo. To be sure, a rather pointed observation must be added here. Curiosity about the creator of an artwork arises only when that image leaves a lasting impression on our minds. Yet, when we look at such works, like the tiger pictured in the Tiger Brand paper advertisement, the clumsy illustrations of tigers’ faces on matchboxes, or a very poorly drawn wrestler standing empty-handed next to a lion, we feel that not knowing the artists behind such works is no loss at all.

For some reason, I have always felt that Prafulla Kumar Lahiri, or Piciel or Kahi Khan, probably outshone everyone else in making the tiger the central character of cartoon-style advertising art, both in execution and in the sheer originality of the concepts behind those illustrations. The way he brought this majestic creature to life in cigarette advertisements is beyond compare in every sense. Even though a subtle European influence lingers in the artwork, its indigenous spirit and caricature belong to an entirely different dimension.

In this context, I must mention the consecutive ‘Passing Show’ cigarette advertisements published in Bengali newspapers, featuring masterfully realistic drawings of animals. Of course, I did not find any tigers there; instead, I found bears and monkeys. Those advertisements depicted townspeople and suburban residents watching bears and monkeys perform, their mouths wide open. Judging by the attire of the characters, one can easily guess that these pictures were probably not drawn by a Bengali artist.
 
An unknown artist depicted traditional bear shows and monkey dances in cigarette advertisements, while Jagadish Dhar's striking illustrations for Tinopal demonstrated the imaginative possibilities of animal imagery in commercial advertising.

Generally, I wish to keep only the works of Bengali artists within the scope of this discussion, even if they appeared in English-language advertisements. In truth, discussing every single work by artists from outside Bengal is difficult within the space available. Yet, when advertisements created by artists from outside Bengal regularly appeared in Bengali newspapers, some mentions become essential, not least because Bengalis took immense delight in viewing them. Take the ‘Passing Show’ illustrations, for instance, though I could not discover the artist's name. The artist was likely someone working for an advertising agency in Mumbai.

These ‘Passing Show’ advertisements began appearing in Bengali newspapers in the late 1930s. Remarkably, the smoker was never the focus of any of them. One could merely spot a lit cigarette in the mouth of some random character amidst the crowd. A discerning viewer would certainly not miss it. And the subject matter? Thoroughly indigenous. Bengalis, too, have witnessed bear shows and monkey dances. The body language of the characters in the drawings reveals the artist's extraordinary powers of observation. The posture of an elderly person leaning forward while watching a monkey dance in a frock is something one cannot even imagine drawing without being an absolute master of the craft!
 
Animal illustrations were common in circus and pet food advertisements, but their appearance in advertisements for unrelated products often reflected remarkable creativity and originality.

One must remember that the use of animal illustrations in print advertisements has a very long history. In the beginning, notices published to find lost livestock or pets would sometimes feature pictures. Circus advertisements were unthinkable without animal images. Yet, the trend of choosing animals as brand icons began in the late nineteenth century. A well-known example is the picture of Nipper, the dog sitting with ears pricked in front of a gramophone. Coming to more recent times, a pug became immensely popular through an advertisement for a mobile phone company. Subsequently, demand for this particular breed skyrocketed among those wishing to keep a dog as a pet. Later, that same mobile phone company even featured a Chihuahua in one of its advertisements. Of course, that was no drawing, but a television commercial. An important character in an advertisement for a famous American insurance company is an animated gecko.
Over time, animal characters featured in advertisements for major brands, including dogs, geckos and polar bears, became immensely popular and widely recognisable.

Advertisements for pet food and pet care brands naturally feature pictures of animals. But novelty comes into play when a car company makes a polar bear the central character of its campaign, or when a battery manufacturer chooses a cat. For this essay, however, I was searching for animal illustrations in Bengali advertisements. The renowned artist Ranen Ayan Dutta often created series of illustrations based on different themes for his famous hair oil advertisements. One such series was based on the tales of the Panchatantra.

I remember that, in my family, children were never encouraged to read comics. The elders believed that once someone became addicted to reading comics, they would develop a sort of aversion to reading real books. Naturally, no one bought me comics like Handa-Bhonda or Batul the Great during my childhood. Now I realise that reading those Panchatantra tales through the hair oil advertisements gave us exactly the same joy as reading comics. Once I had read one story, I would eagerly await the next. But what drew me to those stories in the first place were Ranen Ayan's incredible illustrations. In fact, the stories of the Panchatantra had nothing whatsoever to do with hair oil, yet those pictures and texts seemed to remind consumers of that particular brand over and over again.

The year is 1799. A notice appears in the Calcutta Gazette. Somewhere in Lalbazar, inside the courtyard of an Englishman’s residence, a magnificent tigress from the Sundarbans and her cubs are held in a cage. Citizens are invited to witness the spectacle. The admission fee is a modest eight annas, collected by the keeper of the beasts. One wonders how many curious souls parted with their coins back then to catch a glimpse of the ‘bagh-mama’.

Looking back across the centuries, one can only wish the advertisement had featured a picture of the tiger. Even today, we could have feasted our eyes on it.

The year is 1857. A notice is published in the Sambad Prabhakar by Darogah Brojomohon Roy. A chowkidar from Badamtala police station has captured a ‘Lalmohan’ bird. Should any rightful owner come forward, the bird can be claimed at the station. A modern researcher hazards a guess. The bird likely belonged to some affluent gentleman of contemporary Calcutta. Perhaps, he suggests, the advertisement was placed in the hope of receiving a reward upon its return. Perhaps so. Yet, even here, how thrilled we would have been to behold a picture of ‘Lalmohan-babu’, safely kept in the darogah’s custody!

The year is long gone, yet the practice is familiar. Advertisements for the sale of horses in those days invariably featured woodcut illustrations.

More often than not, these notices were issued by the Calcutta auctioneers Cook & Company. The horse advertisements would meticulously detail how long the animals could endure in battle or whether they possessed the stamina for the racecourse. Atop the notices for horses imported from Australia, a neat little engraving of a horse would sit proudly. Elephants were traded just as readily in this bustling market of majestic beasts. Yet, when an elephant was sold at official government rates, there was no picture to accompany it. One simply had to read the words and imagine its beauty and fine training, much like that old ‘bagh-mama’ or our dear ‘Lalmohan-babu’.
 
A strange-looking tiger in a 1922 rasogolla advertisement, a crudely drawn man fighting a lion on a matchbox, and a remarkably lifelike tiger illustrated by Protul Bandyopadhyay for a gun advertisement in the 1930s.

The year is 1922. A unique advertisement appears in newspapers, featuring the most bizarre drawing of a tiger one could ever encounter. Even John Lawson, the missionary artist of Pashwabali, would surely have smiled at the sight of it. It is not a full-body portrait of the beast, but merely its face. One might playfully remark that the tiger looks precisely like an elderly uncle relaxing in an easy chair. The accompanying copy offers plenty of amusement, too. It boldly claims that these rasogollas are stored in such airtight tins that “even if you open the tin after ten years, you will find them fresh.” Imagine the sheer magnitude of the falsehoods printed in advertisements back then!

I am not here to judge which promotions were sheer fraud and which were not. Nor do I intend to nitpick the artistic flaws of bygone eras. My sole endeavour is to trace the qualitative evolution of animal illustrations in Bengali advertisements across this subcontinent.

Bengalis have gazed upon illustrations of tigers since time immemorial. Their majestic terror runs riot across the pages of Bengali literature. A comprehensive list would have no end. Who has not drawn them? From Haridas Sen and Upendra Kishore Raychowdhury to countless modern artists.

The unforgettable Tuntunir Boi is a treasure trove of vivid imagery: a fox tying a tiger by the tail to make it leap twenty-five yards; a tiger fleeing at the crash of a breaking pot; a tiger dressed as a bridegroom; a tiger tied to a stake, and so many more. These illustrations etched themselves into our minds, driven less by their artistic perfection than by the sheer pull of the tales. We have even beheld Nandalal Bose’s sketch gifted to Satyajit Ray, depicting the tiger whose tail-tip gets scorched in the hearth while trying to steal cooked meat. In Sahajpath, Nandalal once again showed us what a tiger in the wild truly looks like. How much more can one recount?

The long and short of it is simple. One can safely close one's eyes and swear that no one except the artist himself could ever have witnessed a tiger like the one in that advertisement from the Bagbazar sweet company. Consider Rabindranath's famous rhyme about a plump tiger with dark stripes who wanders into a room to eat the bearer, encounters a mirror, and flees in terror at his own reflection, roaring angrily over why his body is covered in black stripes
(“এক ছিল মোটা কেঁদো বাঘ,/ গায়ে তার কালো কালো দাগ।/ বেহারাকে খেতে ঘরে ঢুকে/ আয়নাটা পড়েছে সমুখে।/ এক ছুটে পালালো বেহারা,/ বাঘ দেখে আপন চেহারা।/ গাঁ গাঁ করে ডেকে ওঠে রাগে,/ দেহ কেন ভরা কালো দাগে”).

We also remember the tiger illustration by Nandalal Bose in the book Chitra-Bichitra. That tiger, drawn by Nandalal Bose, is not realistic at all; rather, it is created in the style of our folk art and ancient sculptures, bearing no resemblance to the real tigers we see in zoos. We know that these pictures were not drawn from life; they came from the pure imagination of the artists.
